label: P1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P1}Let $A$ be a Banach lattice algebra and $f\in A^{\prime}$. The
following are equivalent.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $f\in\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)$.

\item[(2)] For every norm bounded disjoint sequence $(x_{n})$, one has
$\left\Vert f\circ x_{n}\right\Vert \longrightarrow0$ in $A^{\prime}$.

\item[(3)] For every norm bounded disjoint sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$
and every positive sequence $(y_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $B_{A}$, we have
\[
\lim\limits_{n\longrightarrow\infty}f(y_{n}x_{n})=0\text{.} 
\]

\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2) follows from the standard characterization of
$L$-weakly compact subsets of a Banach lattice, see \cite[Theorem
5.63]{Aliprantis} or \cite[Proposition 3.6.3]{Meyer}.

(2)$\Longrightarrow$(3) This implication is straightforward.

(3)$\Longrightarrow$(2) Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists a
disjoint sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset$ $B_{A}$ such that
$(\left\Vert f\circ x_{n}\right\Vert )_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ does not converges to
zero. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that there exists
some $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\left\Vert f\circ x_{n}\right\Vert
\geq\varepsilon$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we
can choose $0\leq y_{n}\in B_{A}$ such that $\left\vert f\circ x_{n} 
\right\vert (y_{n})\geq\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}.$ Using the classical
Kantorovich formula
\[
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\leq\left\vert f\circ x_{n}\right\vert (y_{n} 
)=\sup\left\{  \left\vert f\circ x_{n}(z)\right\vert :0\leq z\leq
y_{n}\right\}  \text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}\text{,} 
\]
there exists $0\leq z_{n}\leq y_{n}$ such that $\left\vert f\circ x_{n} 
(z_{n})\right\vert =\left\vert f(z_{n}x_{n})\right\vert \geq\dfrac
{\varepsilon}{4}$. This contradicts (3).

label: Main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Main}Let $A$ be a Banach lattice.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If the dual space $A^{\prime}$ has an order continuous norm, then for
every Banach lattice algebra product $p$ on $A$, \textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(} 
A)=A^{\prime}$.

In particular, if $A^{\prime}$ has an order continuous norm then, $A$ equipped
with any product, is Arens regular.

\item If the dual space $A^{\prime}$ has the PSP then, for every Banach
lattice algebra product $p$ on $A$,
\[
\mathcal{L}\text{-}\mathrm{wap(}A)=\mathrm{wap(}A)=A^{\prime}.
\]


\item If for every Banach lattice algebra product $p$ on $A$, $\mathcal{L} 
$-\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)=A^{\prime}$ then $A^{\prime}$ has an order
continuous norm.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ \ \ 

\begin{enumerate}
\item Assume that $A^{\prime}$ has an order continuous norm. Then $A^{\prime}$
is weakly sequentially complete. Let $0\leq f\in A^{\prime}$ and consider a
sequence $(g_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$\ in the orbit $O_{f}$\ of $f$. Then there
exists a sequence $(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $\left\Vert x_{n}\right\Vert
\leq1$ such that $g_{n}=f.x_{n}$. Since $A^{\prime}$ has order continuous
norm, it follows from \cite[Theorem 5.28]{Aliprantis} that $(g_{n} 
)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ admits a weak Cauchy subsequence. Consequently,
$(g_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. By
Eberlein-Smulian Theorem, $O_{f}$ is relatively weakly compact. Therefore,
$f\in$\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)$.

\item Assume that $A^{\prime}$ has the PSP then $A^{\prime}$ has an order
continuous norm. Let $p$ be a Banach lattice algebra product on $A$, and let
$0\leq f\in A^{\prime}$. By the first point the orbit $O_{f}$ is actually
relatively weakly compact subset. According to \cite[Theorem 4.34] 
{Aliprantis}, if $(g_{n})\subset S(O_{f})$ is a disjoint sequence then it
converges weakly to zero and, by the PSP, it converges to zero in norm. Thus
$f\in\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)$.

\item Assume that $\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)=A^{\prime}$ for
every Banach lattice algebra product $p$ on $A$. To show that $A^{\prime}$ has
order continuous norm, it suffices to prove that every norm bounded disjoint
sequence in $A$ converges weakly to zero. Let $(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a
disjoint sequence in $B_{A}$. Consider a positive functional $0\leq\varphi\in
A^{\prime}$ with $\left\Vert \varphi\right\Vert =1$ and define the product
$.:A\times A\longrightarrow A$ by $x.y=\varphi(y)x$. Then $A$, equipped with
this product becomes a Banach lattice algebra. Let $f\in A^{\prime}$, for
every $x\in A$, the action of $f\circ x$ is given by $f\circ x=f(x)\varphi$.
Since $f\in\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{$wap$}$\mathrm{(}A)$, $\left\Vert f\circ
x_{n}\right\Vert =\left\vert f(x_{n})\right\vert \longrightarrow0$. Therefore,
$x_{n}\longrightarrow0$ weakly in $A$. This shows that $A^{\prime}$ has an
order continuous norm.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $A$ be a Banach $f$-algebra. Then \textrm{$wap$}$(A)=A^{\prime}$ , and
consequently $A$ is Arens regular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $A$ has a unit element. Then its dual space $A^{\prime}$ has
an order continuous norm (see \cite[Theorem 3.3]{depagter}). By Theorem
\ref{Main}, this implies that \textrm{$wap$}$(A)=A^{\prime}$.

If $A$ is semiprime $f$-algebra. Then $A$ is continuously embedded in the
unital Banach algebra $\mathcal{Z}(A)$, via the mapping $x\longmapsto\pi_{x}$
where $\pi_{x}:y\longmapsto xy$. Since $\mathcal{Z}(A)$ is Arens regular, $A$
is Arens regular, because every subalgebra of an Arens regular algebra is
Arens regular (\cite[Corollary 1.4.12]{Palmer}).

In the general case, let $N$ denote the set of all nilpotent elements in $A$
and let
\[
M=N^{\perp}=\left\{  x\in A:x\perp n\text{ for all }n\in N\right\}
\]
be the disjoint complement of $N$. Then $M$ is a semiprime $f$-algebra, and
moreover it satisfies $xy\in M$ for all $x,y\in A$ (see \cite[Proposition
10.2]{BD}). Let $f\in A^{\prime}$ and denote by $g=f_{/M}$ its restriction to
$M$. Let $(x_{n})$ and $(y_{n})$ be two sequences in the closed unit
ball$\ B_{A}$, and assume that the iterated limits
\[
\lim_{n}\lim_{m}f(x_{n}y_{m})=\alpha\text{ and }\lim_{m}\lim_{n}f(x_{n} 
y_{m})=\beta\text{ } 
\]
exist. Since $x_{n}y_{m}\in M$, we have $f(x_{n}y_{m})=g(x_{n}y_{m})$ for all
$n,m\in\mathbb{N}$. By the semiprime case, $g\in\mathrm{wap}(M)$, hence
$\alpha=\beta$, so $f\in\mathrm{wap}(A)$. Consequently, $A$ is Arens regular.

label: le
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{le}The closed solid convex hull $CSCH(X)$ of an $L$-weakly compact set
$X$ in a Banach lattice $E$ is $L$-weakly compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from the stability of $L$-weak compactness under solid convex
hulls and norm closure.
head: environment

label: P3
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{P3}For Banach lattices $A$ and $B$,
\[
B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B}=CSCH(B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}),
\]
where
\[
B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}=\left\{  x\otimes y:0\leq x\in B_{A}\text{, }0\leq
y\in B_{B}\right\}
\]
\qquad
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is clear that $B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}\subseteq B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B}$ and hence $CSCH(B_{A}\otimes B_{B})\subseteq
B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B}$. For the reverse inclusion, it is
enough to show that every $u$ $\in A\overline{\otimes}B$ satisfying
$\left\Vert u\right\Vert \leq1$ belongs to $CSCH(B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}})$.
First, consider $u\in A\overline{\otimes}B$ with $\left\Vert u\right\Vert <1$.
The definition of the positive projective norm gives positive vectors
$x_{k}\in A$ and $y_{k}\in B$ such that $\left\vert u\right\vert \leq 
                                   
               
{\displaystyle\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}}
             
x_{k}\otimes y_{k}$ and $ 
                                   
               
{\displaystyle\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}}
             
\left\Vert x_{k}\right\Vert \left\Vert y_{k}\right\Vert <1$. Let
$x_{i}^{\prime}=\dfrac{x_{i}}{\left\Vert x_{i}\right\Vert }$, $y_{i}^{\prime
}=\dfrac{y_{i}}{\left\Vert y_{i}\right\Vert }$ and $\lambda_{i}=\left\Vert
x_{i}\right\Vert \left\Vert y_{i}\right\Vert $. Then $\left\vert u\right\vert
\leq 
                                   
               
{\displaystyle\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}}
             
\lambda_{k}x_{k}^{\prime}\otimes y_{k}^{\prime}$ with $\lambda_{k}\geq0$ and $ 
                                   
               
{\displaystyle\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}}
             
\lambda_{k}<1$. Therefore $u$ belongs to the solid convex hull $CH(B_{A^{+} 
}\otimes B_{B^{+}})$ of $B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}$. Now, if $\left\Vert
u\right\Vert =1$, the sequence $((1-\frac{1}{n})u)$ is contained in
$SCH(B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}})$ and converges to $u$, hence $u\in
CSCH(B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}})$. It follows that the closed unit ball of
$A\overline{\otimes}B$ is contained in $CSCH(B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}})$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Two vectors $(x,y)$ and $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ in $A\times B$ are said to
be sporadically disjoint if $x\perp x^{\prime}$ or $y\perp y^{\prime}$.

A sequence $(x_{n},y_{n})$ in $A\times B$ is called sporadically disjoint
sequence if for $n\neq m$ the pairs $(x_{n},y_{n})$ and $(x_{m},y_{m})$ are
sporadically disjoint .
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $x\otimes y$ and $x^{\prime}\otimes y^{\prime}\in A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B$. Then $x\otimes y\perp x^{\prime}\otimes y^{\prime}$ if and
only if $(x,y)$ and $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ are sporadically disjoint.

title: Proof
body_md:
(1)$\Longrightarrow$(2) follows from the fact that $W_{f}\subseteq O_{f}$ and
$O_{f}$ is $L$-weakly compact.

(2)$\Longrightarrow$(1) Assume that $W_{f}$ is $L$-weakly compact. Using the
linearity and the continuity of the operator $T_{f}:A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B\longrightarrow(A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert
}B)^{\prime}$ defined by $T_{f}(u)=f.u$ and  proposition \ref{P3}, we obtain
\[
O_{f}=T_{f}(B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B})=T_{f}(CSCH(B_{A^{+} 
}\otimes B_{B^{+}}))\subseteq CSCH(W_{f})
\]
By Lemma \ref{le}, $CSCH(W_{f})$ is $L$-weakly compact, hence $O_{f}$ is
$L$-weakly compact, and therefore $f\in\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{wap} 
$(A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B)$.

(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3) The set $W_{f}$ is $L$-weakly compact if and only if,
for all disjoint sequence $(g_{n})\subseteq S(W_{f})$ converges uniformly to
zero on $B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B}$, that is,
\[
\left\Vert g_{n}\right\Vert =\sup\limits_{u\text{ }\in B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B}}\left\vert g_{n}(u)\right\vert \longrightarrow0
\]
Using the universal property of the Fremlin projective tensor product
\[
\left\Vert g_{n}\right\Vert =\sup\limits_{x\in B_{A^{+}},y\in B_{B^{+}} 
}\left\vert g_{n}(x\otimes y)\right\vert \longrightarrow0
\]
for every disjoint sequence $(g_{n})_{n}\subseteq S(W_{f})$. Thus, $(g_{n})$
converges uniformly to zero on $B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}$. By \cite[theorem
5.63]{Aliprantis}, this is equivalent to the fact that for every disjoint
sequence $(x_{n}\otimes y_{n})\in B_{A^{+}}\otimes B_{B^{+}}$, we have
\[
\sup_{h\in W_{f}}\left\vert h(x_{n}\otimes y_{n})\right\vert =\sup_{x\in
B_{A},\text{ }y\in B_{B^{+}}}\left\vert f.x\otimes y(x_{n}\otimes
y_{n})\right\vert \longrightarrow0
\]
Thus,$W_{f}$ is $L$-weakly compact if and only if for every positive
sporadically disjoint $(x_{n},y_{n})\subset B_{A\times B}$ and every sequence
$(x_{n}^{\prime},y_{n}^{\prime})\subseteq B_{A\times B}$
\[
f(x_{n}^{\prime}x_{n}\otimes y_{n}^{\prime}y_{n})\longrightarrow0\text{.} 
\]
This completes the proof.

label: F
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the unitization of the Banach $f$-algebra $\ell^{1}$, that is
$A=\ell^{1}\oplus\mathbb{R}1$, where $1=(1,1,...)$, with the coordinatewise
order, multiplication
\[
(x+\alpha1)(y+\beta1)=xy+\alpha x+\beta y+\alpha\beta1.
\]
and norm $\left\Vert x+\alpha\right\Vert =\left\Vert x\right\Vert
_{1}+\left\vert \alpha\right\vert $. Then $A$ is a commutative unital Banach
lattice algebra. Since \textrm{$wap$}$(A)=$\textrm{$wap$}$(\ell^{1})\oplus
$\textrm{$wap$}$(\mathbb{R})=A$, $A$ is Arens regular. The Banach $f$-algebra
$c_{0}$ is also Arens regular. We now show that $A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }c_{0}$ is not Arens regular.

Define the bilinear map $\varphi:A\times c_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ by
\[
\varphi(x+\alpha1,g)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{k}g_{k}\text{ for all
}x+\alpha1\in A\text{ and }g\in c_{0}\text{,} 
\]
since $\left\vert \varphi(x+\alpha,g)\right\vert \leq\left\Vert g\right\Vert
_{\infty}\left\Vert x\right\Vert _{1}\leq\left\Vert x+\alpha\right\Vert
\left\Vert g\right\Vert _{\infty}$, $\varphi$ induces a continuous linear
functional, still denoted by $\varphi$, on $A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }c_{0}$, that is
\[
\varphi((x+\alpha1)\otimes g)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{k}g_{k}\text{ for
all }x+\alpha1\in A\text{ and }g\in c_{0}\text{,} 
\]
For $n\geq1$, define
\[
e_{n}=(0,0,..,0,\overset{n}{\overbrace{1}},0,..)\text{, }x_{n}=e_{n}+1\in
A\text{ and }g_{n}=(\overset{n\text{ terms}}{\overbrace{1,1,..1},}0,0..)\in
c_{0}.
\]
and set $u_{n}=\dfrac{x_{n}}{2}\otimes e_{n}\in A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }c_{0}$ and $v_{m}=1\otimes g_{m}\in A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }c_{0}$ for all $n,m\geq1$. Since $\left\Vert u_{n}\right\Vert
_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }=\left\Vert \dfrac{x_{n}}{2}\right\Vert
\left\Vert e_{n}\right\Vert _{\infty}=1$ and $\left\Vert v_{m}\right\Vert
_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }=\left\Vert 1\right\Vert \left\Vert
g_{m}\right\Vert _{\infty}=1$, the sequences $(u_{n})$ and $(v_{m})$ belong to
$B_{A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }c_{0}}$. Moreover,
\begin{align*}
\varphi(u_{n}v_{m}) &  =\varphi(\dfrac{x_{n}}{2}.1\otimes e_{n}g_{m} 
)=\varphi(\frac{1}{2}(e_{n}+1)\otimes e_{n}g_{m})\\
&  =\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}e_{n,k}^{2}g_{m,k}\\
&  = 
                                                                           
               
\genfrac{\{}{.}{0pt}{0}{0\text{ if }n>m}{\frac{1}{2}\text{ if }n\leq m} 
             
\end{align*}
Thus, we obtain
\[
\lim_{n}\lim_{m}\varphi(u_{n}v_{m})=\frac{1}{2}\text{ and }\lim_{m}\lim
_{n}\varphi(u_{n}v_{m})=0\text{.} 
\]
The iterated limits are different. Hence, $\varphi$ is not weakly almost
periodic, and consequently, $A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }c_{0}$ fails
to be Arens regular.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $A$ and $B$ be a Banach lattice algebras. Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ have the PSP, then $A\otimes
_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$ is Arens regular.

\item If $\mathcal{L}^{r}(A,B^{\prime})$ has an order continuous norm, then
$A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$ , $A$ and $B$ are Arens regular.

\item If $A$ and $B$ are Banach $f$-algebras, then $A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B$ is Arens regular.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ \ 

\begin{enumerate}
\item Assume that $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ have the PSP. By \cite[Theorem
1]{Pedro}, it follows that $\mathcal{L}^{r}(A,B^{\prime})=(A\otimes
_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B)^{\prime}$ has the PSP. Hence, by Theorem
\ref{Main}, $\mathcal{L}$-\textrm{$wap($}$A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert
}B)=(A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B)^{\prime}$ which implies that
$A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$ is Arens regular.

\item This follows from Theorem \ref{Main}.

\item If $A$ and $B$ are Banach $f$-algebras, then by \cite[Theorem
4.2]{Jaber}, the Fremlin projective tensor product $A\otimes_{\left\vert
\pi\right\vert }B$ is again a Banach $f$-algebra. Since every Banach
$f$-algebra is Arens regular, the result follows.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $A$ and $B$ be Banach lattice algebras. Their projective tensor product
$A\otimes_{\pi}B$ is a Banach algebra. According to \cite[Remark 3.4]{Jaber},
there exists a unique continuous algebra homomorphism $\theta:A\otimes_{\pi
}B\longrightarrow A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$ which extends the
identity on the algebraic tensor product $A\otimes B$. A natural question
arises about the injectivity of $\theta$.

We show that, in general, the answer is negative. Indeed, let $K$ and
$K^{\prime}$ be compact Hausdorff spaces, each containing a perfect set (that
is, a closed subset without isolated points). Set $A=C(K)$ and $B=C(K^{\prime
})$. Since $A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$ is a Banach $f$-algebra,
it is Arens regular. Suppose, contrary to the claim, that $\theta$ is
injective. Then $A\otimes_{\pi}B$ would be isomorphic, as a Banach algebra, to
the subalgebra $\theta(A\otimes_{\pi}B)$ of the Arens regular algebra
$A\otimes_{\left\vert \pi\right\vert }B$. Consequently, $A\otimes_{\pi}B$
would be Arens regular. However, by \cite[Theorem 6.11]{Lij}, $C(K)\otimes
_{\pi}C(K^{\prime})$ is not Arens regular under the above assumptions on $K$
and $K^{\prime}$. This contradiction shows that $\theta$ cannot be injective.
head: environment
